A designated Board Certified Radiologist will read testing images and provide a descriptive report of their 
interpretation to the ordering or referring LIP.
Radiologists are always encouraged to use their good judgment to determine if the result is critical and 
should be communicated immediately to the referring physician or service. Diagnoses requiring immediate

Documentation of all direct communication is suggested to be a part of the report dictation.
When findings are communicated to a referring LIP's representative, accurate receipt of the findings will be 
confirmed by by the radiologist. The radiologist will note the date, time, and name of the person receiving 
the report.
Direct communication may be accomplished in person or by telephone to the referring LIP or an appropriate 
representative.
In those situations in which the interpreting radiologist feels that immediate patient treatment is indicated 
(e.g. , acute intracranial hemorrhage), the interpreting physician will communicate directly with the referring 
physician or an appropriate representative. If that individual cannot be reached, the interpreting physician 
will directly communicate the need for emergent care to the patient or responsible guardian.
When a preliminary report is given prior to preparation of the final report, any significant change between 
the preliminary report and final interpretation will be directly reported to the appropriate LIP.
Radiology Results and Critical Communication
To provide quality of care and radiology results to Licensed Independent Provider (LIP) or representative to insure 
timely care of patient.
All radiology services such as (CT, x-ray, nuclear medicine, fluoroscopy, MRI, ultrasound, etc) performed will be read 
by a qualified and credentialed physician. The interpretation to such testing is stipulated in the physicians 
delineations. 
A qualified physician may include a surgeon, physiatrist, radiologist, or any other physician that has been 
credentialed and has specific radiology interpretation stipulated in his or her physician's delineation.

IODINATED CONTRAST MEDIA IN RENAL IMPAIRMENT  
This statement, updated in 2025, is based on the March 2020 Consensus Statements from the American College 
of Radiology and the National Kidney Foundation (Davenport, et. al. with full citation below). Throughout the 
following document, much of the text of the reference is quoted verbatim, with the specific page number of the 
included text provided. 
BACKGROUND 
Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) is synonymous with the term post contrast acute kidney injury 
that has been used in the radiology literature and published guidelines. CA-AKI is a general term that describes 
a sudden deterioration in renal function that occurs within 48 hours following the intravascular administration 
of iodinated contrast media. CA-AKI may occur regardless of whether the contrast medium was the cause of the 
deterioration [1, 2]. 
Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI) is now the preferred term for what in the past has been referred 
to as contrast induced nephropathy in the radiology literature. CI-AKI is a specific term used to describe CA-AKI 
caused by the intravascular administration of contrast media after the exclusion of other factors. This definition 
is difficult because most studies have not included a control group of matched patients who were not exposed 
to contrast media, making it difficult to distinguish a correlative relationship (CA-AKI) from a causative one (CI- 
AKI). At the current time, it is the position of ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media that CI-AKI is a real, 
albeit rare, entity, far less common than CA-AKI [1, 2]. 
Multiple patient-related risk factors have been associated with CA-AKI. The primary risk factor is pre-existing 
severe renal impairment with an eGFR less than 30 mL/min. Some studies found an additive risk of CA-AKI from 
diabetes mellitus. Additional risk factors include nephrotoxic agents and exposures, hypotension, hypovolemia, 
albuminuria, and impaired kidney perfusion (e.g., congestive heart failure) (Davenport, p. 662). Patients with 
AKI are also at significant risk and in these patients the eGFR will lag behind the renal impairment and is not 
reliable. 
Few studies have linked patient-related risk factors with CI-AKI. In studies that found evidence of CI-AKI, the 
primary risk factor was eGFR. No other putative risk factors that increase CI-AKI risk beyond eGFR alone have 
been confirmed in well-controlled studies of intravenous media (Davenport, p. 662). 
FOOTNOTES AND CONSIDERATIONS OF SPECIFIC CIRCUMSTANCES 
1. Use of iodinated contrast for emergent examinations: Patients with CKD stages 4 or 5 have a relative rather
than absolute contraindication to iodinated contrast media. If contrast media administration is required for
a life-threatening diagnosis, then it should not be withheld based on kidney function (Davenport, p. 663-
664).
2. Considerations for anuric patients on maintenance dialysis: Because of the inherent demonstrated lack of
benefit, risks, and cost, neither acute dialysis nor continuous renal replacement therapy should be initiated

or have the schedule changed solely based on iodinated contrast media administration, regardless of 
residual kidney function (Davenport, p. 663). Therefore, administration of iodinated contrast does not 
require coordination with or modification of a patient’s routinely scheduled dialysis. 
 
3. Considerations for nonanuric patients on maintenance dialysis: Nonanuric patients undergoing 
maintenance dialysis, whether peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis, are at increased risk of further loss of 
residual kidney function following nephrotoxic exposure(s)… Therefore, nonanuric patients with residual 
kidney function undergoing maintenance dialysis are considered similar to patients with AKI or eGFRs less 
than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 not undergoing dialysis with respect to the potential nephrotoxic risk of iodinated 
contrast media (i.e., relative contraindication). If loss of residual kidney function is considered clinically 
important, then the risks, benefits, and alternatives should be considered, and the need for the procedure 
may require discussion between the referring professional and radiologist (Davenport, p. 664).Note: The 
risk for these non anuric dialysis patients is theoretical that they may be converted to anuric patients with 
contrast exposure.  Non anuric patients still produce 1 -2  cups urine per day ( 100 ml ) as described 
below.   Based on the guidelines, this is not an absolute contraindication but treated similar to patients 
with eGFR of less than 30 where risk vs benefits would need to be assessed. 
Even small residual function confers major benefits: 
 Better volume and BP control 
 Lower phosphate, potassium, and β₂-microglobulin levels 
 Improved nutritional status 
 Fewer hospitalizations 
 Better overall survival 
So losing RRF → worse metabolic control and more dialysis dependence. 
 
4. Administration of iodinated contrast in the setting of acute illness: Acute clinical risk factors (e.g., volume 
depletion) without known AKI are beyond the scope of radiology practices to determine and are left to 
referring clinicians to evaluate. In general, when stable, eGFR is the best indicator of a patient’s potential 
risk of CI-AKI (Davenport, p. 663). Examples of clinical risk factors that warrant consideration include 
dehydration, sepsis, vomiting, diarrhea, suspected acute kidney disease, or acute cardiac disease. Chronic 
illnesses such as cancer are not considered an acute illness, but some chemotherapy regimens may be 
nephrotoxic and may warrant monitoring of eGFR (see below) (Davenport, p. 664). 
 
5. What patient risk factors should trigger eGFR measurement? A personal history of kidney disease (e.g., 
CKD, remote AKI, kidney surgery, kidney ablation, albuminuria) is the most useful element that 
demonstrates a requirement for kidney function determination. Diabetes mellitus is an optional factor for 
screening. Patient age and both treated and untreated hypertension are of uncertain utility as independent 
triggers for kidney function assessment during radiology point of care; they are sensitive indicators and 
confer a large false-positive rate to the identification of patients with eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 
(Davenport, p. 663). Patients with a single normal or partially functioning kidney (e.g., kidney agenesis, 
nephrectomy, transplant) should be managed similarly to patients with normal kidney volume (e.g., two 
normal kidneys). In patients with a single normal or partially functioning kidney, clinical risk should be 
determined based on overall kidney function (i.e., eGFR) and clinical circumstances (i.e., AKI). The presence 
of a solitary functioning kidney should not influence decision making regarding the risk of CA-AKI or CI-AKI

(Davenport, p. 664). In addition, monitoring eGFR in patients receiving nephrotoxic medications (e.g., 
aminoglycosides) or undergoing chemotherapy is important before, during, and after treatment to identify 
incident nephrotoxicity (e.g., AKI or new eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) (Davenport, p. 664). 
6. Considerations for patients receiving nephrotoxic medications or undergoing chemotherapy:

In general, recommendations should not be altered in patients receiving nephrotoxic
medications or undergoing chemotherapy. This is especially true for patients who have normal
eGFR or mild-to- moderate reductions in eGFR because they are not considered at risk,
regardless of the drug(s) prescribed (Davenport, p. 664).

Monitoring eGFR in patients receiving nephrotoxic medications (e.g., aminoglycosides) or
undergoing chemotherapy is important before, during, and after treatment to identify incident
nephrotoxicity (e.g.,

AKI or new eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) (Davenport, p. 664). 
 
 In patients with AKI or eGFRs less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, it may be prudent to withhold nonessential 
potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, diuretics, amino- 
glycosides, amphotericin, platins, zoledronate, methotrexate) if clinically feasible for 24 to 48 hours 
before and 48 hours after exposure (Davenport, p. 664). 
 
 If CA-AKI develops, then nonessential nephrotoxic medications should continue to be withheld until 
kidney function has recovered. In some cases, withholding a nephrotoxic drug or the delay of an 
indicated imaging examination while waiting for an administered nephrotoxic drug to be eliminated may 
carry more risk than the potential risk of CI-AKI. Therefore, decisions regarding the suspension of 
medications should be individualized by referring and other treating providers (Davenport, p. 666). 
7. Considerations for patients with eGFR < 30 (CKD 4 or 5): Patients with CKD stages 4 or 5 (eGFRs of 15–29 
mL/ min/1.73 m2 or less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, respectively) who are not undergoing maintenance 
hemodialysis are at potential risk of CI-AKI. This constitutes relative rather than absolute contraindication to 
iodinated contrast media. If intravenous iodinated contrast media administration is clinically indicated, then 
its use should be informed by consideration of the potential risks and benefits as well as alternative imaging 
strategies. If the decision is made to administer iodinated contrast media in this setting, then volume 
expansion with normal saline is indicated if there are no contraindications (Davenport, pp. 663-664). 
Because of the inherent demonstrated lack of benefit, risks, and cost, acute dialysis… should not be 
initiated… solely based on iodinated contrast media administration, regardless of residual kidney function 
(Davenport, p. 663). 
 
8. Guidelines for hydration/prophylaxis: 
 Based on data for the general prevention of CA-AKI rather than CI-AKI specifically, prophylaxis is 
indicated for patients who have AKI or an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and are not undergoing 
maintenance dialysis (Davenport, p. 663). 
 Prophylaxis is not indicated for the general population of patients with stable eGFR greater than or 
equal to 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, for patients undergoing chronic dialysis, or for patients at risk for heart 
failure (Davenport, p. 663). 
 In individual high-risk circumstances (e.g., numerous risk factors, recent AKI, borderline eGFR), 
prophylaxis may be considered in patients with eGFR of 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m2 at the discretion of the 
ordering clinician (Davenport, p. 663). 
 The risks of prophylaxis (e.g., heart failure, other hypervolemic conditions) should be considered before 
initiation (Davenport, p. 663). 
 Post-procedural prophylaxis may be considered if a study has an emergent indication that does not 
allow sufficient time for preprocedural prophylaxis, although there is no data to support this (Davenport, 
p. 663). 
 When prophylaxis is indicated, isotonic volume expansion with normal saline is the preferred method. 
The ideal timing, volume, and rate of volume expansion is uncertain. Typical volume expansion regimens 
begin 1 hour before and continue 3–12 hours after contrast media administration, with typical doses

ranging from fixed (e.g., 500 mL before and after) to weight-based volumes (1–3 mL/kg per hour). 
Longer regimens (approximately 12 hours) have been shown to lower the risk of CA-AKI compared with 
shorter regimens. However, longer intravenous protocols are generally impractical in the outpatient 
setting (Davenport, p. 663). 
 Oral hydration can be considered for outpatients, although it has not been studied for patients with 
eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. A typical regimen would be 500 mL of water over 2 hours prior to the scan 
and 500 mL of water over 2 hours after scan, with the option to substitute Gatorade or salty fluids. 
 
9. Consider cessation of nonessential potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g. nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs, diuretics, amino- glycosides, amphotericin, platins, zoledronate, methotrexate) if clinically feasible for 
24 to 48 hours before and 48 hours after exposure to possibly decrease the risk of CA-AKI (Davenport, p. 
664). Decisions regarding the suspension of medications should be individualized by referring and other 
treating providers. 
 Bicarbonate is likely similar to normal saline for the prevention of CA-AKI but is not preferred because it 
requires compounding by a pharmacist (Davenport, p. 663). 
 N-acetylcysteine was not shown to be effective versus placebo in a randomized trial of intra-arterial 
iodinated contrast media (Weisbord, et. al. N Engl J Med 2018). 
 
10. Should the dose of iodinated contrast media for CT be reduced in patients at risk for CI-AKI? There is no 
data that implies a dose-ranging toxicity for intravenous administration within the range of clinically 
administered doses. Consequently, if iodinated contrast media is administered to a patient at risk, then a 
conventional single diagnostic dose should be used (i.e., volume typically used for a single diagnostic dose). 
Ad hoc contrast media dose reductions as an effort to mitigate risk of CI-AKI should be avoided because this 
practice may produce a suboptimal or nondiagnostic study. If lower doses of contrast media have been 
shown to be sufficiently diagnostic with specific protocols, then practices should consider lowering doses in 
all patients imaged with those protocols, not only patients with reduced kidney function (Davenport, p. 
664). 
 
11. Metformin and iodinated contrast: Metformin does not increase risk of CA-AKI, but if CI-AKI develops in a 
patient receiving metformin, the patient is at risk for metformin-associated lactic acidosis. Therefore, in 
accordance with US FDA recommendations, metformin should be withheld from patients with severe renal 
impairment (eGFR less than 30 mL/ min) or with AKI at the time of the exam and for at least 48 hours 
afterwards until return of baseline renal function. Metformin does not need to be withheld in patients 
without AKI and with eGFR greater than or equal to 30 mL/min (Davenport, p. 666).

depletion) without known AKI are beyond the scope of radiology practices to determine and are left to
referring clinicians to evaluate. In general, when stable, eGFR is the best indicator of a patient’s potential
risk of CI-AKI (Davenport, p. 663). Examples of clinical risk factors that warrant consideration include
dehydration, sepsis, vomiting, diarrhea, suspected acute kidney disease, or acute cardiac disease. Chronic
illnesses such as cancer are not considered an acute illness, but some chemotherapy regimens may be
nephrotoxic and may warrant monitoring of eGFR (see below) (Davenport, p. 664).
5. What patient risk factors should trigger eGFR measurement? A personal history of kidney disease (e.g.,
CKD, remote AKI, kidney surgery, kidney ablation, albuminuria) is the most useful element that
demonstrates a requirement for kidney function determination. Diabetes mellitus is an optional factor for
screening. Patient age and both treated and untreated hypertension are of uncertain utility as independent
triggers for kidney function assessment during radiology point of care; they are sensitive indicators and
confer a large false-positive rate to the identification of patients with eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2
(Davenport, p. 663). Patients with a single normal or partially functioning kidney (e.g., kidney agenesis,
nephrectomy, transplant) should be managed similarly to patients with normal kidney volume (e.g., two
normal kidneys). In patients with a single normal or partially functioning kidney, clinical risk should be
determined based on overall kidney function (i.e., eGFR) and clinical circumstances (i.e., AKI). The presence
of a solitary functioning kidney should not influence decision making regarding the risk of CA-AKI or CI-AKI
RP Statement on Iodinated Contrast Media
(Davenport, p. 664). In addition, monitoring eGFR in patients receiving nephrotoxic medications (e.g.,
aminoglycosides) or undergoing chemotherapy is important before, during, and after treatment to identify
incident nephrotoxicity (e.g., AKI or new eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) (Davenport, p. 664).
6. Considerations for patients receiving nephrotoxic medications or undergoing chemotherapy:
In general, recommendations should not be altered in patients receiving nephrotoxic
medications or undergoing chemotherapy. This is especially true for patients who have normal
eGFR or mild-to- moderate reductions in eGFR because they are not considered at risk,
regardless of the drug(s) prescribed (Davenport, p. 664).
Monitoring eGFR in patients receiving nephrotoxic medications (e.g., aminoglycosides) or
undergoing chemotherapy is important before, during, and after treatment to identify incident
RP Statement on Iodinated Contrast Media
AKI or new eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) (Davenport, p. 664).
 In patients with AKI or eGFRs less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, it may be prudent to withhold nonessential
potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, diuretics, amino-
glycosides, amphotericin, platins, zoledronate, methotrexate) if clinically feasible for 24 to 48 hours
before and 48 hours after exposure (Davenport, p. 664).
 If CA-AKI develops, then nonessential nephrotoxic medications should continue to be withheld until
kidney function has recovered. In some cases, withholding a nephrotoxic drug or the delay of an
indicated imaging examination while waiting for an administered nephrotoxic drug to be eliminated may
carry more risk than the potential risk of CI-AKI. Therefore, decisions regarding the suspension of
medications should be individualized by referring and other treating providers (Davenport, p. 666).
7. Considerations for patients with eGFR < 30 (CKD 4 or 5): Patients with CKD stages 4 or 5 (eGFRs of 15–29
mL/ min/1.73 m2 or less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, respectively) who are not undergoing maintenance
hemodialysis are at potential risk of CI-AKI. This constitutes relative rather than absolute contraindication to
iodinated contrast media. If intravenous iodinated contrast media administration is clinically indicated, then
its use should be informed by consideration of the potential risks and benefits as well as alternative imaging
strategies. If the decision is made to administer iodinated contrast media in this setting, then volume
expansion with normal saline is indicated if there are no contraindications (Davenport, pp. 663-664).
Because of the inherent demonstrated lack of benefit, risks, and cost, acute dialysis… should not be
initiated… solely based on iodinated contrast media administration, regardless of residual kidney function
 Based on data for the general prevention of CA-AKI rather than CI-AKI specifically, prophylaxis is
indicated for patients who have AKI or an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and are not undergoing
 Prophylaxis is not indicated for the general population of patients with stable eGFR greater than or
equal to 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, for patients undergoing chronic dialysis, or for patients at risk for heart
 In individual high-risk circumstances (e.g., numerous risk factors, recent AKI, borderline eGFR),
prophylaxis may be considered in patients with eGFR of 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m2 at the discretion of the
 The risks of prophylaxis (e.g., heart failure, other hypervolemic conditions) should be considered before
 Post-procedural prophylaxis may be considered if a study has an emergent indication that does not
allow sufficient time for preprocedural prophylaxis, although there is no data to support this (Davenport,
 When prophylaxis is indicated, isotonic volume expansion with normal saline is the preferred method.
The ideal timing, volume, and rate of volume expansion is uncertain. Typical volume expansion regimens
begin 1 hour before and continue 3–12 hours after contrast media administration, with typical doses
RP Statement on Iodinated Contrast Media
ranging from fixed (e.g., 500 mL before and after) to weight-based volumes (1–3 mL/kg per hour).
Longer regimens (approximately 12 hours) have been shown to lower the risk of CA-AKI compared with
shorter regimens. However, longer intravenous protocols are generally impractical in the outpatient
 Oral hydration can be considered for outpatients, although it has not been studied for patients with
eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. A typical regimen would be 500 mL of water over 2 hours prior to the scan
and 500 mL of water over 2 hours after scan, with the option to substitute Gatorade or salty fluids.
9. Consider cessation of nonessential potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g. nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs, diuretics, amino- glycosides, amphotericin, platins, zoledronate, methotrexate) if clinically feasible for
24 to 48 hours before and 48 hours after exposure to possibly decrease the risk of CA-AKI (Davenport, p.
664). Decisions regarding the suspension of medications should be individualized by referring and other
 Bicarbonate is likely similar to normal saline for the prevention of CA-AKI but is not preferred because it
requires compounding by a pharmacist (Davenport, p. 663).
 N-acetylcysteine was not shown to be effective versus placebo in a randomized trial of intra-arterial
iodinated contrast media (Weisbord, et. al. N Engl J Med 2018).
10. Should the dose of iodinated contrast media for CT be reduced in patients at risk for CI-AKI? There is no
data that implies a dose-ranging toxicity for intravenous administration within the range of clinically
administered doses. Consequently, if iodinated contrast media is administered to a patient at risk, then a
conventional single diagnostic dose should be used (i.e., volume typically used for a single diagnostic dose).
Ad hoc contrast media dose reductions as an effort to mitigate risk of CI-AKI should be avoided because this
practice may produce a suboptimal or nondiagnostic study. If lower doses of contrast media have been
shown to be sufficiently diagnostic with specific protocols, then practices should consider lowering doses in
all patients imaged with those protocols, not only patients with reduced kidney function (Davenport, p.
11. Metformin and iodinated contrast: Metformin does not increase risk of CA-AKI, but if CI-AKI develops in a
patient receiving metformin, the patient is at risk for metformin-associated lactic acidosis. Therefore, in
accordance with US FDA recommendations, metformin should be withheld from patients with severe renal
impairment (eGFR less than 30 mL/ min) or with AKI at the time of the exam and for at least 48 hours
afterwards until return of baseline renal function. Metformin does not need to be withheld in patients
without AKI and with eGFR greater than or equal to 30 mL/min (Davenport, p. 666).

September 1, 2015 
 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
Revised Policy Effective:  Immediately 
 
Policy change in regards to CAT Scans (CT) of the Chest With and/or Without Contrast.  This 
change will affect both interpreting radiologists and performing technologists.     
 
Patients with a current diagnosis, a follow-up diagnosis, or any history of: 
• Pulmonary Nodules 
• Cancer 
• Suspected Nodules in the Chest 
 
An Axial MIPS (Maximum Intensity Projection) series should be performed in addition to the 
standard sequences.  MIPS sections should have a 2 mm spacing with a 15 mm thickness.   
 
 The primary clinical application of MIPS is to improve the detection of pulmonary 
nodules.  MIPS also helps characterize the distribution of small nodules. 
 
To continue to provide the utmost care for our patients, please apply these new requirements 
to your workflow.  Feel free to contact me or Medical Imaging Associates staff with any 
additional questions or concerns. 
 
 
Thanks in Advance for Your Cooperation, 
 
 
 
 
John J. Strobel M.D., President 
Medical Imaging Associates of Idaho Falls

November 16, 2015 
 
 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
In reference to the recent change in the American Cancer Society (ACS) guidelines for 
mammography.  Medical Imaging Associates want to clarify their continued adherence to the 
guidelines set by the American College of Radiology (ACR), for mammography.  If the ACR 
makes changes that coincide with ACS guidelines, further information will be sent out at that 
time. 
 
Remind patients that it is important to discuss their individual health and concerns with their 
ordering physician.  It is the responsibility of the treating physician to determine the best course 
of treatment considering each patient's individual circumstances.   
 
As a facility, take advantage of this opportunity to increase awareness and educate the 
individuals in your community about breast health.  October has ended, and even though it can 
be a crazy time for breast imaging, this is a great way to keep that momentum moving forward 
and increase volume in screening mammography.   
 
Sincerely, 
John J. Strobel M.D., President 
Medical Imaging Associates of Idaho Falls

Peter L. Vance, M.D., President                                  Justin A. Lamb, D.O., Sr. Vice President                                   Steven A. Larsen, M.D., Vice President 
          James B. Harris, M.D., Secretary                                   Richard W. Bentley, M.D., Treasurer                                   Michael P. Hodel, Chief Operating Officer 
 
December 2018 
 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
 
Medical Imaging Associates (MIA) is striving to strengthen processes involving patient care.  Listed are three to four 
points of emphasis in our standard operating procedures for breast imaging.  These standards were discussed at 
our breast conference on Oct 9, 2018. 
 
1. Biopsy marking clips should be placed after all biopsies. 
2. Post-biopsy mammograms should be performed on all biopsies, regardless of modality used to 
perform the biopsy. 
3. (Actually, part of #2) Patient should not leave until the radiologist has seen the post biopsy 
mammogram images. 
4. If you perform a biopsy on a patient who already has a marker in her breast or you perform a two-site 
biopsy, a marker with a different shape should be used to mark the biopsy site. 
 
A more detailed explanation for each of these items is provided below. 
 
1. Biopsy marking clips should be placed after all biopsies. 
o 
What about axillary lymph node biopsies? 
 Yes.  
 Positive axillary lymph node biopsy no longer means definitive axillary LN dissection.  
 Many surgeons may opt to perform a lumpectomy + removal of the positive axillary 
node. 
 
 Clip is needed in axillary node to target for localization. 
 
 Expect to see this more and more in coming years. 
 
o 
Only exception should be if the patient adamantly refuses after extensive explanation. The patient 
   should understand that not placing a marker may result in: 
 1.) Additional future biopsies 
 2.) Limited treatment options 
 3.) Increased need for mastectomy 
 
2. Post-biopsy mammograms should be performed on all biopsies, regardless of modality used to 
perform the biopsy. 
 
CONTINUED… 

 
 
 
          Peter L. Vance, M.D., President                                  Justin A. Lamb, D.O., Sr. Vice President                                   Steven A. Larsen, M.D., Vice President 
          James B. Harris, M.D., Secretary                                   Richard W. Bentley, M.D., Treasurer                                   Michael P. Hodel, Chief Operating Officer 
 
3. (Actually, part of #2) Patient should not leave until the radiologist has seen the post biopsy 
mammogram images.  
o 
Why? 
 To confirm that the area biopsied was the intended target initially seen on breast 
   imaging.  
 If the area biopsied is not concordant then an additional biopsy is needed, possibly with 
a different breast imaging method. 
 
 To confirm the correct location of the clip. 
 If the clip migrates - its position and distance from the biopsy site should be 
documented on the day of the biopsy.    
 
 To confirm clip deployment. 
 Occasionally, clips don't deploy.  
 If the clip doesn't deploy, go back to the biopsy room and place the clip. 
 
 If the biopsy is positive, post biopsy mammogram images will be used for planning the 
   localization. 
 
4. If you perform a biopsy in a patient who already has a marker in her breast or perform a two-site 
biopsy, a marker with a different shape should be used to mark the biopsy site. 
o 
Using the same clip for 2 different sites could result in localization/excision of the wrong site. This 
   is a well-documented complication. 
 
o 
Currently, most of our sites only have 1 type of clip. Efforts are underway to have multiple types 
   of clips available at each location. 
 
o 
Until then - consider using the stereo biopsy clips for US guided biopsies (the shape is different  
   - not a ribbon). The stereo clip device won't fit through the Bard introducer, but you can remove  
   the introducer and insert the stereo clip device directly. 
 
o 
If no additional shape is available, in the meantime, still place a marker and include a thorough  
  documentation of location with measurements in your report for future care.  
 
 
 
Thank you! 
 
Dr. M. Enslow and Dr. S. Parker

MIA Screening Mammo Protocol 
Updated 09-19-2024 
The goal of mammography is the detection, characterization, and evaluation of findings 
suggestive of breast cancer and other breast diseases. It is important for an individual to 
discuss their breast health and concerns with their primary care provider. 
 
The American College of Radiology has set practice parameters for annual screening 
mammography as indicated below:  
 
1. Annual mammograms are recommended for women age 40 and older who have no 
current problems and are at an average risk for breast cancer. 
 
2. Women under the age of 40, who have no current problems but have an increased risk 
for breast cancer, may begin annual screening mammography starting around age 30. These 
women of higher risk include: 
 Women with known mutation or genetic syndrome with increased breast cancer risk. 
o  Annually starting by age 30, but not before age 25. 
  Untested women with a first-degree relative with known BRCA mutation. 
o Annually starting by age 30, but not before age 25. 
 Women with a 20% or greater lifetime risk for breast cancer based on breast cancer risk 
models. 
o Annually starting by age 30, but not before age 25, or 10 years earlier than the 
age at which the youngest first-degree relative was diagnosed, whichever is 
later. 
 Women with a history of chest (mantle) radiation received between the ages of 10 and 
30. 
o Annually starting 8 years after the radiation therapy, but not before age 25. 
 Women with biopsy-proven lobular neoplasia, atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH), ductal 
carcinoma in-situ (DCIS), invasive breast cancer, or ovarian cancer should begin annual 
screening from the time of diagnosis, regardless of age.

09-19-2024: Screening Mammogram Updates 
Effective immediately, for screening mammograms we will be omitting the 2D mammogram 
from the protocol. We will only be performing a tomosynthesis and synthetic 2D view or c-view 
and not a 2D mammogram.  
There is abundant data showing that omitting the 2D has no effect on cancer detection rates. 
Benefits include cutting unnecessary radiation, shorter exam times, and fewer images to 
interpret.  
This applies only to follow up routine screening mammograms.  
A 2D image with tomosynthesis and synthetic view will still be performed with baseline 
screening exams and all diagnostics.  
If your machine does not have the capability or the software package to create the synthesized 
2D view, please continue using your current protocol.

ON TABLE

•  40cc ultrasound gel per vagina (female patients)

Standard Breast MRI 
Sequences: 
1.Localizer 
2.In phase sequence 
3.T2 w fat sat 
4.Inversion recovery sequence 
5.T1 fat sat precontrast 
6.T1 fat sat post contrast x 3  
■   Inject contrast. Scan ﬁrst pass immediately (no delay) 
■   Scan 2nd pass immediately when 1st pass ﬁnishes. 
■   Scan 3rd pass immediately when 2nd pass ﬁnishes. 
■   *Send precontrast, post contrast pass 1, pass 2, and pass 3 each separately to PACS (ie not stacked 
or interleaved, but each as their own independent sequence in PACS). 
■   *Send SUBTRACTED post contrast pass 1, 2, and 3 each separately to PACS (ie there should be 3 
individual separate subtracted sequences in PACS). 
■   *Send sagiƩal                           reconstrucƟon of post con pass 2. 
■   *Send sagiƩal reconstrucƟon of SUBTRACTED post con pass 2. 
7.MIP series 
■    Axial MIP of the subtracted pass 1, subtracted pass 2, and subtracted pass 3 (total of 3 MIP images). 
These need to be STACKED, so that they are in PACS as 1 series - 1st          image is sub pass 1 MIP, 2nd 
image is sub pass 2 MIP, 3rd image is sub pass 3 MIP. 
 
Speciﬁc parameters for the T1 fat sat precon and the T1 fat sat post contrast images are as follows: 
■   3D acquisiƟon 
■   1 mm slices 
■   ConƟguous with no gap 
■   FOV: 300 mm 
■   Matrix: 300 x 300 
■   Voxel size: 1 x 1 x 1mm

Christopher O. Harker, M.D., President 
Richard W. Bentley, M.D., Sr. Vice President 
J. Fritz Schmutz, M.D., Vice President 
Nicholas S. Pierson, M.D., Secretary 
Matthew E. Williamson, D.O., Treasurer 
Michael P. Hodel, Chief Executive Officer 
Medical Imaging Associates (MIA) policy regarding GAD 
Contrast Agent for MRI Scans: 
 
Assessment of Risk (See Table 1 for the classification of GBCAs)  
Group II agents  
Based on the most recent scientific and clinical evidence the ACR Committee on Drugs and 
Contrast Media considers the risk of Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) among patients 
exposed to standard or lower than standard doses of group II Gadolinium-based contrast agent 
(GBCA) are sufficiently low or possibly nonexistent such that assessment of renal function with a 
questionnaire or laboratory testing is optional prior to intravenous administration. As in all 
instances, group II GBCAs should only be administered if they are deemed necessary by the 
supervising radiologist, and the lowest dose needed for diagnosis should be used as deemed 
necessary by the supervising radiologist.1  
 
Group I and III agents  
The ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media concludes that patients receiving group I 
GBCAs should be considered at risk of developing Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) if any of 
the following conditions apply to the patient:  
• 
On dialysis (of any form)  
• 
Severe or end-stage CKD (CKD 4 or 5, eGFR < 30 mL / min/1.73 m2) without dialysis  
• 
AKI  
There is insufficient real-life data to determine the risk of NSF from administration of group III 
agents, despite an alternative excretion pathway for hepatobiliary agents. Thus, it is important to 
identify patients at risk of developing NSF, as defined above, prior to injection of group I and III 
GBCAs. The method used to identify such patients may differ for outpatients versus inpatients.  
 
Identifying at-risk outpatients  
Outpatients who may be receiving group I or group III agents should be screened for conditions 
and other factors that may be associated with renal function impairment. The following list of risk 
factors can be used to identify patients who have impaired renal function:  
• History of renal disease, including:  
◦ Dialysis  
◦ Kidney transplant  
◦ Single kidney  
◦ Kidney surgery  
◦ History of known cancer involving the kidney(s)  
◦ History of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) or prior history of Acute Kidney 
Infection (AKI) 
• History of diabetes mellitus (optional)  
 
Once an outpatient is identified as being at risk for having reduced renal function based on 
screening, and group I or group III GBCA administration is contemplated, renal function should 
be assessed by laboratory testing (checking results of prior laboratory tests performed within an 

 
Christopher O. Harker, M.D., President 
Richard W. Bentley, M.D., Sr. Vice President 
J. Fritz Schmutz, M.D., Vice President 
Nicholas S. Pierson, M.D., Secretary 
Matthew E. Williamson, D.O., Treasurer 
Michael P. Hodel, Chief Executive Officer 
acceptable time window and ordering new laboratory tests only if necessary) and calculation of 
Glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). However, if the patient is on dialysis or has known AKI, 
laboratory testing and calculation of eGFR is not useful or necessary (i.e., eGFR is not accurate in 
this setting, and these patients would be considered at risk for NSF prior to group I or group III 
administration regardless of calculated eGFR).  
 
Calculating eGFR  
For adults, eGFR calculation is commonly performed using the Modification of Diet in Renal 
Disease (MDRD) equation or the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-
EPI) equation.  
 
Identifying at-risk inpatients  
For all inpatients, an eGFR level should be obtained within 2 days prior to planned administration 
of a group I or group III GBCA. In addition, ordering health professionals should assess 
inpatients for the possibility of AKI, as eGFR calculation alone has limited accuracy for the 
detection of AKI.  
 
Patients with CKD 4or5 (eGFR<30mL/min/1.73m2) not on chronic dialysis  
Group I agents are contraindicated in this setting. If a GBCA-enhanced MRI study is to be 
performed, a group II agent should be used.  
 
Patients with CKD 3 (eGFR 30 to 59 mL / min/1.73 m2)  
NSF developing after GBCA administration to patients with stable eGFR 30-59 ml/min/1.73 m2 is 
exceedingly rare. No special precautions are necessary in this group [48,49].  
 
Patients with CKD 1or2 (eGFR60to119mlmin/1.73m2)  
There is no evidence that patients in these groups are at increased risk of developing NSF. Any 
GBCA can be administered safely to these patients.  
 
 
TABLE 1. ACR Manual Classification of Gadolinium-Based 
Agents Relative to Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis 
 
Group I: Agents associated with the greatest number of NSF cases:  
Gadodiamide (Omniscan® – GE Healthcare)  
Gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist® – Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals)  
Gadoversetamide (OptiMARK® – Guerbet)  
 
Group II: Agents associated with few, if any, unconfounded cases of NSF:  
Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance® – Bracco Diagnostics)  
Gadobutrol (Gadavist® – Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals; Gadovist in many countries) Gadoteric acid 
(Dotarem® – Guerbet, Clariscan – GE Healthcare)  
Gadoteridol (ProHance® – Bracco Diagnostics)

J. Fritz Schmutz, M.D., Vice President 
Nicholas S. Pierson, M.D., Secretary 
Matthew E. Williamson, D.O., Treasurer 
Michael P. Hodel, Chief Executive Officer 
 
Group III: Agents for which data remains limited regarding NSF risk, but for which few, if any unconfounded 
cases of NSF have been reported:  
                Gadoxetate disodium (Eovist – Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals; Primovist in many countries)  
 
 
TABLE 2. eGFR Evaluation of Renal Function to Group I or Group III 
GBCA Administration

eGFR Requirement

No eGFR required — eGFR is not helpful in this situation.

No eGFR required — eGFR is not helpful in this situation.

time the MR exam is scheduled 
If NO risk factors [1], no eGFR required.  
WITH risk factors [1], obtain eGFR.*

If NO risk factor [1] and eGFR of 60 or above, no new eGFR required.

within 6 weeks of the MRI, no new eGFR is needed; otherwise obtain a

of the MRI exam, as per the last line in the table.

Based on the most recent scientific and clinical evidence the ACR Committee on Drugs and
Contrast Media considers the risk of Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) among patients
exposed to standard or lower than standard doses of group II Gadolinium-based contrast agent
(GBCA) are sufficiently low or possibly nonexistent such that assessment of renal function with a
questionnaire or laboratory testing is optional prior to intravenous administration. As in all
instances, group II GBCAs should only be administered if they are deemed necessary by the
supervising radiologist, and the lowest dose needed for diagnosis should be used as deemed
The ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media concludes that patients receiving group I
GBCAs should be considered at risk of developing Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) if any of
the following conditions apply to the patient:
Severe or end-stage CKD (CKD 4 or 5, eGFR < 30 mL / min/1.73 m2) without dialysis
There is insufficient real-life data to determine the risk of NSF from administration of group III
agents, despite an alternative excretion pathway for hepatobiliary agents. Thus, it is important to
identify patients at risk of developing NSF, as defined above, prior to injection of group I and III
GBCAs. The method used to identify such patients may differ for outpatients versus inpatients.
Outpatients who may be receiving group I or group III agents should be screened for conditions
and other factors that may be associated with renal function impairment. The following list of risk
factors can be used to identify patients who have impaired renal function:
◦ History of known cancer involving the kidney(s)
◦ History of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) or prior history of Acute Kidney
Once an outpatient is identified as being at risk for having reduced renal function based on
screening, and group I or group III GBCA administration is contemplated, renal function should
be assessed by laboratory testing (checking results of prior laboratory tests performed within an

acceptable time window and ordering new laboratory tests only if necessary) and calculation of
Glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). However, if the patient is on dialysis or has known AKI,
laboratory testing and calculation of eGFR is not useful or necessary (i.e., eGFR is not accurate in
this setting, and these patients would be considered at risk for NSF prior to group I or group III
For adults, eGFR calculation is commonly performed using the Modification of Diet in Renal
Disease (MDRD) equation or the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-
For all inpatients, an eGFR level should be obtained within 2 days prior to planned administration
of a group I or group III GBCA. In addition, ordering health professionals should assess
inpatients for the possibility of AKI, as eGFR calculation alone has limited accuracy for the
Patients with CKD 4or5 (eGFR<30mL/min/1.73m2) not on chronic dialysis
Group I agents are contraindicated in this setting. If a GBCA-enhanced MRI study is to be
performed, a group II agent should be used.
Patients with CKD 3 (eGFR 30 to 59 mL / min/1.73 m2)
NSF developing after GBCA administration to patients with stable eGFR 30-59 ml/min/1.73 m2 is
exceedingly rare. No special precautions are necessary in this group [48,49].
There is no evidence that patients in these groups are at increased risk of developing NSF. Any
GBCA can be administered safely to these patients.

January 18, 2016 
 
 
 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
Revised Policy Effective:  Immediately 
 
Policy change in regards to Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the Lumbar Spine With and/or 
Without Contrast.  This change will affect both interpreting radiologists and performing 
technologists.     
 
In patients with a current diagnosis, a follow-up diagnosis, or any history of: 
• Vertebral Diskitis 
• Osteomyelitis 
 
A “Diffusion” scan should be performed, in addition to the standard imaging sequences.  
Diffusion imaging improves differentiation of infectious from degenerative changes of the 
spine. 
 It is possible that additional scan time will be necessary contingent upon the amount of 
levels being evaluated.   
 
To continue to provide the utmost care for our patients, please apply these new requirements 
to your workflow.  Feel free to contact me or Medical Imaging Associates staff with any 
additional questions or concerns. 
 
 
Thanks in Advance for Your Cooperation, 
 
 
 
 
John J. Strobel M.D., President 
Medical Imaging Associates of Idaho Falls

To: Sonographers performing breast ultrasound in ER or Urgent Care settings 
Emergency Breast Ultrasound 
 
Please contact an MIA radiologist on-call for all ER breast ultrasounds. This is for two reasons: 
 
1. Breast ultrasound should be supervised by an MQSA certified breast radiologist as 
additional images may be required. 
 
2. Most ER breast ultrasounds do not filter to a reading list that can be automatically 
seen by the radiologist on call. Communication and case assignment in Clario to the 
radiologist will ensure that the case is read as efficiently as possible.
